questions.question: What are the two types of health checks available in an Auto Scaling Group?
questions.answer: EC2 health checks and ELB (Elastic Load Balancing) health checks. EC2 health checks are always enabled and monitor infrastructure-level status. ELB health checks are optional (but recommended) and monitor application-level HTTP responses.

questions.question: What does the health check grace period do and what is the default value?
questions.answer: The grace period is the amount of time ASG waits after launching a new instance before running health checks on it. This prevents instances from being terminated while they're still booting. The default value is 300 seconds (5 minutes).

questions.question: What is Simple Scaling and when would you use it?
questions.answer: Simple Scaling adds or removes a fixed number of instances when a CloudWatch alarm fires. It has a cooldown period (default 300 seconds) during which no further scaling occurs. It is best used for demos, learning environments, and simple workloads — not for production systems with variable load.

questions.question: What is Step Scaling and how does it differ from Simple Scaling?
questions.answer: Step Scaling uses step adjustments to scale different amounts based on how severely the metric has exceeded the threshold. For example: add 1 instance at CPU 60-70%, add 2 at 70-85%, add 4 at 85%+. Unlike Simple Scaling, it uses instance warmup instead of cooldown, allowing faster response to escalating load.

questions.question: What is Target Tracking Scaling?
questions.answer: Target Tracking lets you define a target metric value (e.g., keep CPU at 50%) and AWS automatically manages the instance count to maintain that target. You don't define how many instances to add or remove — AWS handles it like a thermostat for your infrastructure.

questions.question: What is Predictive Scaling and when is it useful?
questions.answer: Predictive Scaling uses machine learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and proactively launch instances before expected demand arrives. It's useful when you have at least 2 weeks of traffic data and a recurring traffic pattern — for example, daily lunch-hour spikes or weekly campaign traffic.

questions.question: What is Connection Draining and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Connection Draining (Deregistration Delay) allows in-flight requests to finish before an instance is removed from the Target Group. The Load Balancer stops sending new requests to the draining instance but lets existing ones complete within the configured timeout (default 300s, range 0-3600s). Without it, active user sessions are abruptly terminated when ASG scales in.

questions.question: What is path-based routing in an Application Load Balancer?
questions.answer: Path-based routing routes requests to different Target Groups based on the URL path. For example, /orders goes to the Orders service Target Group and /payments goes to the Payments service Target Group — all via one ALB. This is the foundation of microservices architecture on AWS.

questions.question: What is the default termination policy and what does it do?
questions.answer: The Default Termination Policy first identifies the Availability Zone with the most instances (to maintain AZ balance), then terminates the instance using the oldest Launch Template or configuration. This ensures AZ balance is maintained and the fleet stays on the latest configuration.

questions.question: What are the three CloudWatch alarm states?
questions.answer: OK (metric is within threshold, no action), ALARM (metric has breached threshold, triggers scaling action), and INSUFFICIENT_DATA (not enough data points to evaluate the alarm — common right after creation).

questions.question: Walk me through how you would troubleshoot instances being constantly terminated and replaced in an ASG.
questions.answer: (Situation) Instances were launching and terminating in an infinite loop. (Task) Identify and fix the root cause. (Action) First, I checked the ASG Activity History to see termination reasons — it showed 'Instance failed health check.' I then checked the health check grace period — it was set to 60 seconds. The application logs showed the app took 4 minutes to start. I increased the grace period to 300 seconds and verified the Target Group health check path was returning HTTP 200. (Result) The loop stopped. New instances passed health checks and entered InService state successfully.

questions.question: Your team reports intermittent 503 errors during peak traffic despite EC2 instances all showing healthy. How do you diagnose this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Users getting 503 errors but EC2 health checks show all instances healthy. (Task) Find the root cause. (Action) Since EC2 checks pass but users get errors, I suspected the application layer. I enabled ELB health checks and immediately saw two instances marked Unhealthy in the Target Group — their /health endpoint was returning 503 due to a database connection pool exhaustion. (Result) I fixed the connection pool config, restarted the app on those instances, and they recovered. The 503s stopped. Lesson: always enable ELB health checks in production.

questions.question: Describe how you would configure Auto Scaling for an e-commerce site that experiences both predictable weekday traffic and unpredictable flash sales.
questions.answer: (Situation) E-commerce platform with two traffic patterns: predictable office hours and random flash sales. (Task) Design a robust scaling strategy. (Action) I used a combination of policies. Scheduled Scaling to pre-warm 5 instances every weekday at 7 AM and scale down at 9 PM. Target Tracking Scaling with CPU target at 60% to handle random spikes reactively. I also enabled ELB health checks and set the grace period to 180 seconds. (Result) During normal hours, costs stayed low. During a flash sale, Target Tracking kicked in instantly. No outages.

questions.question: A user is uploading a 200MB file when ASG decides to terminate their instance due to a scale-in action. The deregistration delay is 30 seconds but the upload will take 2 minutes. What happens and how would you prevent this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Long-running upload being terminated mid-stream. (Task) Understand and prevent broken uploads. (Action) With a 30-second drain window, the upload is cut off after 30 seconds regardless of completion status. To fix this, I increased the deregistration delay to at least 180 seconds (preferably matching the max expected upload time). I also added Instance Scale-In Protection on busy instances if the application can detect active uploads, or moved to a pre-signed S3 URL upload pattern where uploads go directly to S3 instead of through EC2. (Result) Users' uploads complete gracefully even during scale-in events.

questions.question: Your ASG has Simple Scaling configured. Traffic suddenly spikes from 20% CPU to 95% in 2 minutes. Why might this be a problem?
questions.answer: (Situation) Rapid CPU spike from 20% to 95%. (Task) Explain Simple Scaling's behavior. (Action) Simple Scaling fires when CPU crosses the threshold (e.g., 70%) and adds a fixed number of instances (say, 2). Then the cooldown period (300 seconds) kicks in. During these 5 minutes, CPU remains at 95% but ASG does nothing — it can't trigger another action during cooldown. After 5 minutes, 2 more instances are added — but by then, users may have already experienced degraded performance for several minutes. (Result) For this scenario, Step Scaling or Target Tracking would be far more appropriate as they respond faster and proportionally to severity.

questions.question: How would you set up path-based routing for a microservices application with three services: Orders, Payments, and Inventory?
questions.answer: (Situation) Three independent microservices needing a unified entry point. (Task) Design the ALB routing architecture. (Action) I created one Application Load Balancer with three Target Groups (Orders-TG, Payments-TG, Inventory-TG). Each Target Group has its own Auto Scaling Group, allowing independent scaling. On the ALB listener, I created three path-based routing rules: /api/orders* → Orders-TG, /api/payments* → Payments-TG, /api/inventory* → Inventory-TG. Each Target Group has its own health check endpoint. (Result) One public ALB endpoint, three independently scaling microservices. Cost-efficient, scalable, and failure-isolated.

questions.question: How does Step Scaling handle rapidly escalating load better than Simple Scaling?
questions.answer: (Situation) Load escalating rapidly in a short time. (Task) Compare both policies under this condition. (Action) With Simple Scaling, each alarm trigger adds a fixed number then blocks further actions for 300 seconds cooldown. Under rapid escalation, you might add 2 instances at T=0, then wait 5 minutes, add 2 more at T=300 — very slow. With Step Scaling, each step fires based on current metric severity, not a time-based block. It uses instance warmup, not cooldown — so if load jumps from 70% to 90%, it can fire the appropriate higher step and add more instances quickly. (Result) Step Scaling responds proportionally and faster to rapidly worsening load.

questions.question: What happens when you enable ELB health checks without first verifying your Target Group health check configuration?
questions.answer: (Situation) ELB health checks enabled without verifying Target Group health endpoint. (Task) Explain the risk. (Action) AWS warns about this in the console: if the health check path doesn't exist or isn't returning HTTP 200 (e.g., /health returns 404), then all instances fail the health check. ASG starts terminating 'unhealthy' instances and launching replacements — which also fail, creating a termination loop. (Result) Enabling ELB health checks without verifying the health endpoint first can take down your entire fleet. Always check the Target Group health check path in the Load Balancer console before enabling.

questions.question: Design an Auto Scaling Group configuration for a globally popular mobile game that sees daily traffic peaks at 7 PM user local time across multiple time zones.
questions.answer: (Situation) Mobile game with rolling time-zone peaks, not a single daily spike. (Task) Design a 24/7 responsive ASG. (Action) Since the peak is always 'happening' somewhere in the world due to time zones, the load is relatively constant globally but shifts in origin. I'd use Target Tracking Scaling with a request-per-instance metric as the primary policy. This continuously adjusts capacity globally. I'd also set appropriate min/max across multiple regions. For each region with a known prime time, I'd layer Scheduled Scaling to pre-warm additional capacity 30 minutes before the regional peak. (Result) No single global spike, so continuous reactive scaling handles most cases. Scheduled pre-warm covers the predictable per-region peaks.

questions.question: How would you use lifecycle hooks to implement blue-green deployment with an Auto Scaling Group?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need zero-downtime blue-green deployment using ASG. (Task) Design the deployment workflow. (Action) Create a Pending:Wait lifecycle hook on the new (green) ASG. When a new instance launches, it enters Wait state and runs a script to deploy the new application version, run smoke tests, and validate readiness. If all tests pass, the script sends a CONTINUE signal to the lifecycle hook, and the instance moves to InService. The ALB target group weight shifts gradually from blue to green. If smoke tests fail, the script sends ABANDON — the instance is terminated without ever joining the fleet. (Result) Only validated instances serve traffic. Bad deployments are caught before any user impact.

questions.question: Explain the trade-offs between using Target Tracking Scaling alone vs a combination of Target Tracking + Step Scaling.
questions.answer: (Situation) Designing scaling strategy for a production system. (Task) Compare single-policy vs multi-policy approach. (Action) Target Tracking alone is great — AWS manages scale-out and scale-in to maintain your target metric. But it's reactive: if a sudden traffic burst causes your metric to spike dramatically in seconds, Target Tracking may not provision capacity fast enough. Adding Step Scaling as a 'fast response' policy for extreme metric values (e.g., if CPU goes above 90%, immediately add 6 instances) gives an aggressive catch-up layer. Both policies can coexist. (Result) Target Tracking handles steady-state and moderate changes. Step Scaling handles extreme sudden spikes. Together, they cover both scenarios better than either alone.

questions.question: What is the risk of setting Connection Draining (Deregistration Delay) too high vs too low?
questions.answer: Too low (e.g., 0-30 seconds): In-flight requests are cut off abruptly. Users experience errors, dropped file uploads, broken API calls. Bad user experience, potential data corruption for non-idempotent operations. Too high (e.g., 3600 seconds): Scale-in becomes very slow. When ASG wants to remove instances, they linger for up to an hour serving new requests that are redirected elsewhere. This delays cost savings and complicates rolling updates. Best practice: set it to match your 95th percentile request duration plus a buffer. For APIs, 30-60 seconds. For file uploads, match the max upload time.

questions.question: How does ASG handle an Availability Zone outage? Which termination policy behavior helps maintain AZ balance?
questions.answer: (Situation) One Availability Zone goes down, instances terminate. (Task) Understand ASG AZ recovery behavior. (Action) When instances in an AZ fail health checks (due to AZ outage), ASG marks them Unhealthy and terminates them. It then attempts to launch replacements — but since the AZ is down, it launches in the remaining healthy AZs. This creates an AZ imbalance (e.g., AZ-A has 6 instances, AZ-B has 2). The Default Termination Policy handles the opposite direction: when the failed AZ recovers and new instances can launch, ASG gradually rebalances by terminating instances in over-provisioned AZs. This is why always configuring ASG across 3+ AZs is a best practice.

questions.question: A startup asks you: 'Should we use Predictive Scaling from day one?' What is your advice?
questions.answer: No — Predictive Scaling requires at least 2 weeks of historical traffic data to generate meaningful forecasts. On day one, there's no history to learn from, so predictions would be inaccurate or disabled. The right approach for a new deployment: start with Target Tracking Scaling as your reactive baseline. Enable CloudWatch detailed monitoring. After 2+ weeks of traffic data accumulates, evaluate whether traffic patterns are recurring and predictable. If they are, enable Predictive Scaling on top of Target Tracking to proactively pre-warm capacity. Never rely on Predictive Scaling alone — always keep a reactive policy as a fallback.

questions.question: Walk me through the full lifecycle of an EC2 instance inside an ASG from launch to termination, including all possible lifecycle hook states.
questions.answer: 1. Pending — ASG decided to launch the instance. Health check grace period starts. Lifecycle hook Pending:Wait pauses here for custom launch scripts. 2. Pending:Proceed — lifecycle hook cleared, instance continues launching. 3. InService — instance passes health checks, registers with the Target Group, begins receiving traffic. 4. Terminating — ASG decides to terminate (scale-in, health check failure, or manual action). Lifecycle hook Terminating:Wait pauses here for cleanup. 5. Terminating:Proceed — cleanup scripts complete or timeout. 6. Terminated — instance is permanently shut down and deregistered. Throughout: health checks run every 30-300 seconds (configurable). ASG maintains desired count by replacing Terminated instances with new Pending instances.
